item.title: RIKEN Team Improves Parallel Control of Silicon Spin Qubits
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article matters because RIKEN’s new control scheme directly tackles the long‑standing crosstalk problem that has limited silicon spin qubits to sequential operation, opening a realistic path toward densely packed, wafer‑scale quantum processors built with existing CMOS infrastructure. By demonstrating high‑fidelity simultaneous gating across multiple spins, the work dovetails with recent Intel and IBM efforts to integrate spin qubits with classical control electronics, suggesting that large‑scale error‑corrected silicon quantum chips could be assembled much sooner than previously thought. The results still rely on cryogenic wiring and precise calibration, so further engineering will be needed before the approach can be deployed in full‑stack architectures.

item.title: Podcast with Johannes Pollanen, Co-founder of EeroQ and a Professor of Physics at Michigan State University
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article spotlights EeroQ’s unconventional qubit design that traps single electrons on a superfluid‑helium film, offering potentially record‑long coherence while still being fabricated on standard semiconductor wafers. By arguing that the proven silicon chip manufacturing ecosystem is essential for scaling, Pollanen links an exotic physics platform to the practical realities of mass production—a key hurdle for any quantum hardware roadmap. The discussion places EeroQ’s approach alongside recent advances in silicon spin qubits and trapped‑ion systems, highlighting a possible hybrid path that could combine ultra‑low decoherence with industrial‑scale integration. Readers should watch how this marriage of novel qubit physics and conventional chip fabrication might reshape the race toward fault‑tolerant quantum computers.

Johannes Pollanen, co-founder of EeroQ and a professor of physics at Michigan State University, explains how EeroQ builds qubits from single electrons floating on a film of superfluid helium, and why he thinks the semiconductor chip is the only proven way to scale a quantum computer. item.title: RIKEN Demonstrates High-Fidelity Simultaneous Control of Silicon Spin Qubits Above 99.9% Threshold
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article reports a milestone for silicon‑based quantum processors by demonstrating simultaneous control of five spin qubits with fidelities exceeding the 99.9 % fault‑tolerance threshold using a single microwave line and a novel calibration scheme that suppresses AC‑Stark crosstalk. By meeting the error‑correction benchmark in a compact, CMOS‑compatible platform, the work builds on recent advances from Intel and other groups that have pushed individual silicon qubit fidelities toward the same level, bringing scalable, chip‑integrated quantum hardware closer to reality. The result is promising for larger arrays, though extending the technique beyond five qubits and integrating full error‑correcting codes will be the next critical challenges.

Researchers at RIKEN and collaborators have achieved high-fidelity simultaneous control of five silicon spin qubits, maintaining over 99.9% accuracy. They overcame crosstalk caused by AC-Stark shifts through a new calibration protocol, enabling the use of a single microwave control line. This breakthrough meets the fault-tolerant threshold for quantum error correction and paves the way for more scalable quantum computers. item.title: MIT Physicists Use First-Principles AI to Resolve Non-Abelian Anyon Order at Strong Landau Level Mixing
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article shows how a self‑attention AI model can finally untangle the long‑standing question of which non‑Abelian anyon order dominates when Landau‑level mixing is strong, confirming the anti‑Pfaffian phase that underpins proposed topological qubits. By delivering a first‑principles computational tool that bridges many‑body physics and machine learning, the work accelerates the design of noise‑resilient platforms such as monolayer WSe₂ and semiconductor quantum wells. It builds on recent experimental hints of non‑Abelian statistics and offers a concrete roadmap for turning those exotic excitations into fault‑tolerant hardware, though practical implementation will still require material quality and temperature control advances.

MIT researchers used a specialized self-attention neural network to solve complex equations related to quantum particles, confirming the existence of anti-Pfaffian topological states. This breakthrough provides a roadmap for building noise-resistant topological qubits in materials like monolayer WSe2 and semiconductor quantum wells. item.title: D-Wave Demonstrates 3D Analog-Digital Quantum Simulation of Higher-Order Topological Insulators Using 728 Qubits
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article shows that D‑Wave’s Advantage2 processor can now run a true three‑dimensional analog‑digital simulation of higher‑order topological insulators on a scale of 728 qubits, marking the first time such bulk topological invariants have been extracted with quantum annealing hardware. By marrying analog annealing with digital control pulses, the work expands the toolbox for programmable condensed‑matter simulators and puts D‑Wave’s platform in direct competition with gate‑model approaches that are still limited to far smaller lattices. The result hints at faster exploration of exotic materials, though it remains confined to Hamiltonians that map naturally onto the annealer’s connectivity and noise profile.

D-Wave has successfully demonstrated 3D analog-digital quantum simulation of higher-order topological insulators using up to 728 qubits on an Advantage2 superconducting quantum annealing processor. This achievement, detailed in a research study on arXiv, involved new analog-digital quantum control protocols to measure localized boundary modes and extract 3D bulk topological invariants. This breakthrough confirms the utility of analog-digital quantum annealing hardware as a programmable simulator for condensed matter physics and topological materials. The move builds on recent trends such as Amazon Braket’s multi‑backend support and IBM’s Qiskit Runtime, signalling that the industry is converging on unified execution layers. However, performance will still depend on each platform’s gate fidelity and connectivity, so benchmarking native Qrisp runs remains essential.

Open Quantum has launched a native Qrisp integration, enabling high-level QPU execution across IonQ, Rigetti, IQM, and AQT hardware. The integration simplifies quantum programming by providing software-engineering abstractions, automated qubit allocation, and memory management. item.title: Chalmers Next Labs, ConScience, and NQFF Validate Superconducting Qubit Chip Stability Across International Testbeds
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article shows that superconducting qubit chips can retain their performance even after being shipped across continents, a milestone for scaling quantum hardware collaborations and supply chains. By proving that the QiB1 processor survives the environmental shifts between Gothenburg and Singapore, the study validates the emerging “cross‑facility measurement service” model that could become a de‑facto standard for benchmarking devices worldwide. It dovetails with recent efforts to create interoperable testbeds such as the WACQT–NQFF Twin Testbed, helping industry move from isolated labs toward a more distributed, commercial quantum ecosystem. The result also reminds readers that while transport stability is now demonstrated, long‑term reliability under repeated handling and varied cryogenic setups will still need systematic monitoring.

A joint study by Chalmers Next Labs AB, ConScience AB, and Singapore’s National Quantum Federated Foundry (NQFF) validated the stability of a superconducting quantum processor (QiB1) when transported between international research facilities. The study, conducted under the WACQT–NQFF Twin Testbed initiative, confirmed that environmental changes between Gothenburg and Singapore did not degrade the processor’s performance. This collaboration is now being commercialized as a standardized cross-facility measurement service. By leveraging native Rydberg interactions rather than gate‑based circuits, Kipu Quantum sidesteps many error‑correction overheads and builds on recent quantum kernel and variational QML studies that have struggled to outperform classical baselines at scale. The results hint that neutral‑atom platforms could become practical accelerators for drug‑discovery pipelines, though broader validation on diverse chemical libraries and comparison with optimized classical models will be needed before industrial adoption.

Kipu Quantum demonstrated a novel method for molecular toxicity classification using analog quantum feature extraction on QuEra's 256-qubit Aquila neutral-atom quantum processor. item.title: Demonstration of Logical Error Suppression in a Surface Code Memory on a Cloud-Accessible IBM Superconducting Processor
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article marks one of the first demonstrations that a surface‑code memory can be run on a publicly accessible superconducting processor with measurable logical error suppression, showing that careful circuit compilation—short readout, fused measurement/reset and an XX echo—can cut per‑round logical errors by up to fourfold. By comparing distance‑3 and distance‑6 layouts on the same hardware, the authors provide concrete evidence that increasing code distance still yields a tangible reduction in logical error rates (≈ 0.5% → 0.2%) even amid realistic qubit‑to‑qubit variation and correlated noise. The work bridges the gap between laboratory‑scale error‑correction experiments and cloud‑based quantum services, suggesting that scalable fault tolerance may be achievable without bespoke hardware upgrades, though long‑lived error correlations remain a key obstacle to be tamed.

Quantum error correction can suppress logical errors exponentially with code distance when physical noise is below threshold. Realizing this on hardware requires tight coordination among quantum gates, mid-circuit measurements, and qubit coherence. Device variation, noise asymmetry, and correlations across space and time complicate the translation of these capabilities into logical error suppression. Here, we study rotated surface-code memory on an IBM Nighthawk r2 processor. Performance varies across tested processor placements, which we attribute to differences in qubit quality. We optimize the code by combining short readout, fused measurement and reset, and an XX echo on data qubits during ancilla readout. Compared with standard readout without reset or echo, the optimized syndrome extraction circuit reduces the median per-round logical error rate by factors of 3.8 in the X basis and 1.4 in the Z basis. In memory experiments of up to 150 rounds, the distance advantage weakens, alongside long-lived correlations that may reflect a persistent error component. Under our optimization recipe, increasing the protected distance from 3 to 6 while holding the other distance fixed reduces the per-round logical error rate from 0.53% to 0.24% in Z memory and from 0.52% to 0.22% in X memory. The corresponding error-suppression factors under maximum-likelihood decoding are 1.68 and 1.85. These results connect circuit compilation and optimization to surface-code memory performance and limitations, and motivate QPU and QEC circuit codesign for fault-tolerant quantum computing primitives on current cloud hardware.

Read original at arXiv Quantum Physics
item.author: Mark Eatherly

item.title: Quality-of-Transmission Estimation in Quantum Networks: Compute, Simulate, or Learn?
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article tackles a bottleneck for future quantum internets by asking how network controllers can quickly gauge the fidelity of entanglement across candidate paths—a metric essential for routing, scheduling and memory management. By adapting the optical‑network quality‑of‑transmission mindset into a compute/simulate/learn framework, it shows that analytical formulas suffice only in trivial regimes, full‑scale simulators are needed when stochastic memory effects dominate, and compact machine‑learning surrogates can deliver near‑real‑time estimates once trained. The work links directly to the growing body of research on quantum network control planes and suggests a practical path toward scalable, low‑latency resource allocation, while warning that data‑generation costs and sim‑to‑real transfer remain open challenges.

Future quantum networks will rely on control-plane decisions such as routing, scheduling, entanglement provisioning, purification, and memory allocation. Each decision depends on a timely and reliable estimate of the quality of the entanglement that a candidate path can deliver, with end-to-end fidelity as a central metric. Inspired by the optical-networking experience with quality-of-transmission (QoT) estimation, this article asks when a quantum controller should compute fidelity analytically, simulate it, or learn a surrogate model. The optical analogy is useful but incomplete: optical QoT estimation often predicts a scalar transmission margin, whereas quantum QoT estimation must account for probabilistic entanglement generation, random memory waiting times, decoherence, state consumption, and measurement constraints that can make fidelity a stochastic target. We propose a compute/simulate/learn framework for quantum QoT estimation and illustrate it with a simulation-based proof of concept. Our study shows that analytical composition can be sufficient in simple regimes, that simulation becomes necessary when stochastic memory effects shape the delivered fidelity distribution, and that lightweight learned surrogates can approximate simulator labels at much lower runtime cost for online control. We close with open challenges for deployment, including stochastic targets, sim-to-real transfer, data-generation cost, physics-informed learning, and generalization beyond individual paths to full network topologies.

By leveraging optically addressable spins deposited directly on a chip, NVision aims to create photonically entangled gates that sidestep some of the cryogenic overhead of superconducting qubits while still targeting fault‑tolerant architectures, echoing recent interest in room‑temperature spin‑photon interfaces from groups at MIT and Oxford. If the integration challenges can be tamed, the technology could accelerate quantum simulation of chemistry and materials by offering a more manufacturable path to large‑scale qubit arrays, though readers should note that coherence times and error rates for molecular spins remain an open question.

NVision Quantum Technologies is expanding from its commercial hyperpolarized MRI platform into quantum computing hardware with its new PIQC (Photonic Integrated Quantum Chip) molecular architecture. This strategy utilizes synthetic organic molecules with optically addressable spin states deposited on silicon photonic chips, aiming for a scalable, photonically-entangled gate architecture for fault-tolerant quantum computing. item.title: Improving the estimation of spin-bath parameters via initial correlations and a two-qubit probe
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article shows that a modest two‑qubit probe—when the second qubit is prepared in a correlated state with the environment—can boost spin‑bath parameter estimation by up to an order of magnitude compared with conventional single‑qubit sensing. By exploiting initial system‑environment correlations rather than direct inter‑qubit coupling, the authors achieve a factor‑3–4 improvement in quantum Fisher information for coupling strength and about eightfold for temperature, highlighting a practical route to more precise noise spectroscopy on solid‑state platforms. The result dovetails with recent interest in correlated probes for quantum metrology, though its impact will depend on experimental ability to engineer and preserve those initial correlations in realistic hardware.

We study how a second qubit can improve the estimation of spin-environment parameters when only one of the two qubits is measured. Both qubits are coupled to a common spin bath through the exactly solvable central-spin model, in which populations and coherences both evolve. Because the bath operator coupled to the qubits commutes with the bath Hamiltonian, the environment induces no effective interaction between the qubits. Without initial correlations or direct inter-qubit coupling, the two-qubit probe therefore performs exactly like a single qubit. When initial system-environment correlations are included, preparing the second qubit reshapes the environment statistics in a parameter-dependent way, and the measured qubit reads out this imprint. This improves the quantum Fisher information (QFI) for the coupling strength by factors of 3-4 relative to a correlated single-qubit probe, and by more than an order of magnitude relative to an uncorrelated one. For temperature estimation, the improvement reaches a factor of about 8. A direct Ising coupling does not help by itself, but the advantage persists in its presence. We also derive the classical Fisher information for arbitrary projective measurements and identify the measurement that saturates the QFI, which in general lies out of the equatorial plane of the Bloch sphere.

item.title: Solving Large-Scale Parameter Inference in Controllable Nuclear Fusion via Coherent Ising Machines and Block Coordinate Descent
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article shows how a Coherent Ising Machine can turn the notoriously slow Bayesian inversion of tokamak plasma parameters into a millisecond‑scale optimization by encoding the MAP problem directly onto an all‑to‑all spin Hamiltonian, leveraging optical parametric oscillators for rapid quantum‑fluctuation–driven search. It builds on recent demonstrations that analog quantum optimizers such as CIMs and D‑Wave can tackle combinatorial problems far faster than classical sampling, extending those capabilities to a high‑impact fusion‑control application. While the current need for block‑coordinate iteration limits true real‑time operation today, the work outlines a clear scaling path that could make closed‑loop plasma control feasible once larger optical networks become available.

Bayesian inference enables self-consistent plasma parameter inversion in tokamak integrated data analysis by fusing multi-source diagnostics. However, under nonlinear Gaussian likelihoods, finding the maximum a posteriori (MAP) estimate typically relies on sampling methods whose high computational overhead precludes real-time plasma control. To address this bottleneck, we propose a Bayesian inversion framework using a Coherent Ising Machine (CIM)-a quantum computing architecture based on coupled degenerate optical parametric oscillators (DOPOs). With native all-to-all connectivity, the CIM directly maps the negative log-posterior potential onto a spin Hamiltonian and leverages quantum vacuum fluctuations for rapid state-space search during pitchfork bifurcation. Validated on plasma current profile inversion for the EAST tokamak, this method achieves a single-run solution time of approximately 1 ms. Although current qubit limits necessitate a block-wise iterative scheme that prevents full real-time execution today, rapidly scaling quantum hardware offers a clear pathway toward real-time tokamak control.

item.title: ConQUESTA: Topology-Aware Post-Training Structural Pruning of Quantum Neural Networks
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article introduces ConQUESTA, a topology‑aware post‑training pruning framework that jointly optimizes task saliency and compiler cost to trim entangling gates in quantum neural networks while guaranteeing an accuracy bound. By evaluating whole‑circuit masks across multiple coupling maps, the method achieves up to 82 % reduction in two‑qubit operations on standard benchmarks—far surpassing simple baseline pruning and dramatically easing the gate‑depth constraints of near‑term hardware. The work signals a practical step toward scalable QNN deployment on sparse superconducting or ion‑trap devices, though its current validation is limited to small (4–12 qubit) models and a handful of datasets.

Deploying quantum neural networks (QNNs) on sparse hardware requires preserving task accuracy while reducing compiler-induced two-qubit gates, SWAPs, and depth. We present ConQUESTA (\underline{C}onstrained \underline{Qu}antum \underline{E}ntangler \underline{S}election with \underline{T}opology \underline{A}wareness), a post training pruning framework that combines task saliency with compiler cost, screens candidate entanglers, and searches complete pruning masks under an explicit accuracy constraint. Unlike one-shot ranking, each mask is transpiled as a whole across multiple coupling topologies. Across 4-, 6-, and 8-qubit QNNs and eight model seeds at 55% pruning, ConQUESTA achieves mean resource reductions of 61.6% on Breast Cancer, 72.0% on Digits01, and 82.2% on Iris, exceeding the strongest matched simple baseline by 3.5, 1.7, and 8.9 percentage points, respectively. Fixed-mask recovery raises feasibility from 16/24 to 22/24 runs. In a fixed-k=4 scaling study on a scaling probe of 4 to 12-qubits, the raw mask space grew from 495 to 12.1M while the evaluated masks increase only from 189 to 305. Resource-weight changes alter depth/routing priorities with at most a 0.44-point mean validation shift.

item.title: SpinControl: Control Software for Prototyping and Benchmarking of Spin-Qubit Devices and Measurement Protocols
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article introduces SpinControl, a purpose‑built control stack that finally bridges the gap between low‑level hardware tuning and high‑level circuit programming for spin‑qubit processors. By cleanly separating data from behavior, modularizing functionality, and embedding CI‑driven robustness, it lets experimental teams prototype new pulse sequences or calibration routines while giving algorithm developers a stable API for running circuits—something that has been missing as silicon‑based qubits scale beyond a handful of dots. The framework’s cloud connectivity, virtual‑gate compilation and spin‑qubit‑specific GUIs could accelerate both device optimization and benchmark reproducibility across labs, positioning spin qubits to compete more directly with superconducting platforms. However, its impact will depend on community adoption and integration with existing hardware stacks, which remain fragmented today.

Quantum computers require software to control the states of the qubits. As the actions on qubits grow in complexity with circuit execution, calibration, and benchmarking, the complexity of the control software grows in tandem. Spin-qubit quantum computers are at a stage where experimentalists need low-level access for tuning and calibration, and quantum algorithm researchers want high-level circuit-level access. In this article, we present the software design of SpinControl. SpinControl integrates three architectural metrics: 1) customizability, to allow prototyping devices and measurement protocols, is achieved by separating data and behaviour; 2) modularity and extensibility are achieved by separating functionalities into different components; and 3) robustness, to reliably execute quantum circuits on many qubits, is achieved by CI pipelines and input validation. SpinControl allows different types of measurements while customizing the instruments used, the pulse or circuit program executed, and the data processing. It allows building standardized experiments from measurement and analysis building blocks and executing these for calibration in a custom and conditional order. SpinControl implements these functionalities alongside robust configuration and data management, a connection to the cloud, and calibration scheduling. Pulse and circuit compilation, virtual gate matrices, as well as spin-qubit-specific GUIs integrated by SpinControl, make heavy use of software packages developed by Delft University of Technology: pulse lib, core-tools (both open source), and QConstruct

item.title: Learning angles for quantum approximate optimization
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article tackles one of QAOA’s biggest practical hurdles—finding high‑quality variational angles—by training a neural model that predicts them directly from the problem graph, turning an expensive per‑instance optimizer into a single forward pass. The approach not only matches solver performance on current quantum hardware but also generalizes to unseen topologies such as Barabási‑Albert and 2D grids, suggesting a scalable route for real‑world combinatorial workloads. By amortizing the data‑generation cost, the method could make QAOA viable for industrial settings where many similar optimization instances must be solved repeatedly.

The Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm (QAOA) and its variants are leading algorithms to help solve challenging combinatorial optimization problems. QAOA maps these problems to Ising Hamiltonians such that their ground state is the desired solution. Candidate solutions are then drawn from a variational quantum circuit. The performance of QAOA hinges on a set of variational angles. However, finding good angles is an instance-specific and computationally expensive non-convex classical optimization task. Here, we learn the mapping from the problem instance to high-quality QAOA angles. Our learned models replace the per-instance optimization, that we call the solver, with a single forward pass that is several orders of magnitude faster than the solver with a near identical quality. Our models further generalize to unseen topologies such as Barabási-Albert and 2D grid graphs. Experiments on quantum hardware confirm that QAOA samples with angles produced by our open-source models are indistinguishable from solver angles. Crucially, models sensitive to the topology of the problem instance increase the quality of the QAOA angles. Our work amortizes a major bottleneck in QAOA by an up-front data generation and training cost. Predicting chemical reactions in biomolecules is challenging because reactive centers are embedded within complex environments that strongly influence their energetics and mechanisms. Here, we present a hybrid quantum-classical workflow that combines molecular dynamics, density functional theory, and correlated wavefunction methods, tightly integrating CPUs, GPUs, and quantum processing units (QPUs) to enable simulations across multiple length and accuracy scales. We apply this approach to ADGRG1 autoproteolysis, a maturation reaction in an adhesion G protein-coupled receptor that has not previously been studied using correlated electronic-structure methods. Our simulations treat a biologically realistic system containing more than one million atoms, including the full-length uncleaved receptor embedded in an endoplasmic-reticulum membrane, while incorporating a 54-qubit IQM quantum processor and up to 1,200 NVIDIA H100 GPUs. These results demonstrate how quantum computers can serve as accelerators within scalable scientific workflows, extending correlated electronic-structure methods to biologically relevant systems.

item.title: Concrete Functions in Private Simultaneous Quantum Messages: Quantum Advantages and Structural Limitations
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article demonstrates that even in the ultra‑minimal private simultaneous quantum messages model, entanglement can cut communication costs for concrete total functions such as three‑party equality and majority well below classical lower bounds, highlighting a genuine quantum advantage with only a handful of qubits. At the same time it uncovers sharp structural limits—most notably the impossibility of a perfectly correct and private protocol for three‑bit AND using just one shared three‑qubit state—showing that not every function benefits from the same shortcut. By pinpointing exactly where entanglement helps and where higher‑dimensional resources are required, the work bridges recent advances in quantum communication complexity with practical considerations for near‑term hardware implementations of secure multiparty protocols.

Private simultaneous quantum messages (PSQM) provide a minimal model of noninteractive secure multiparty quantum computation, yet their communication complexity for concrete functions remains poorly understood. We show that familiar total functions already exhibit both genuine quantum advantages and strong structural limitations. For three-party equality on $n$-bit inputs, which determines whether the players' $n$-bit strings are identical, we construct an entanglement-assisted protocol with asymptotic communication $(1.633\ldots)n$ qubits, whereas every perfectly correct protocol without prior entanglement requires at least $3n$ qubits. For three-bit majority, one shared GHZ state and one transmitted qubit per player suffice for perfect correctness and perfect privacy, reducing the communication from the optimal classical cost of six bits to three qubits. Three-bit AND behaves differently. No perfectly correct and perfectly private protocol exists when the players share an arbitrary three-qubit state, apply arbitrary local unitary encodings, and transmit one qubit each. However, increasing the local dimension overcomes this obstruction: one shared three-qutrit GHZ state and one transmitted qutrit per player yield a one-shot protocol with total communication $3\log_2 3$. Together with the six-bit classical lower bound, this gives a strict quantum communication advantage. More generally, for every $k\geq 3$, we construct a perfectly correct and perfectly private one-shot protocol for $k$-bit AND using one qudit of dimension at most $k$ per player, and hence at most $k\log_2 k$ qubits in total.

item.title: Quantum approximate stochastic combinatorial optimisation
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article tackles a notoriously hard class of problems—two‑stage stochastic combinatorial optimisation—by embedding the scenario‑dependent recourse directly into a variational quantum‑walk circuit, allowing the algorithm to search over first‑stage decisions without explicitly computing costly expected minima. By demonstrating that QASCO concentrates probability on optimal choices more effectively than earlier two‑stage QAOA approaches and can be calibrated with a depth‑independent parameter set that generalises to unseen instances of size beyond 2³², it points toward scalable quantum heuristics for real‑world planning under uncertainty. However, the results are still limited to exact state‑vector simulations, so experimental validation on near‑term hardware will be the next crucial step.

Two-stage stochastic combinatorial optimisation concerns discrete decisions made before all relevant information is known. An initial decision is made; once uncertainty is resolved, it can be adapted to the realised scenario, at a cost. The aim is to find the initial decision that minimises the upfront cost plus the expected cost of optimal adaptation. The first-stage decision problem is often NP-hard, and computing the expected minimum recourse cost can be $\#\mathrm{P}$-hard for a single first-stage candidate. We introduce Quantum Approximate Stochastic Combinatorial Optimisation (QASCO), a variational quantum-walk ansatz that coherently incorporates scenario-dependent recourse into its dynamics to search over first-stage decisions without explicitly evaluating expected minimum recourse costs. We demonstrate QASCO for MaxCut with stochastic edge weights, obtain a circuit with polynomial per-layer gate complexity, and study the ansatz via exact state-vector simulation. Across the instances considered, QASCO concentrates amplitude more effectively on stochastic-optimal first-stage decisions than a previously proposed two-stage QAOA construction. We further show that the ansatz can be calibrated using a depth-independent number of parameters and applied to unseen instances without further circuit-parameter optimisation, including joint decision--scenario--recourse spaces spanning more than $2^{32}$ configurations. Under a query-cost model, comparison with the tested classical heuristics using sample-average approximations of the expected minimum recourse cost shows that QASCO more reliably reaches globally optimal first-stage solutions while requiring fewer cut evaluations. These results show how to incorporate scenario-dependent recourse into the ansatz dynamics, providing a general framework for variational quantum walks in two-stage stochastic combinatorial optimisation.

item.title: Discovering state-of-the-art quantum circuits with large language models
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article shows that large language models can act as creative partners in quantum circuit design, automatically generating reversible architectures that beat the best hand‑crafted solutions on most benchmark tasks. By coupling an LLM proposer with a rigorous evaluator, the authors demonstrate a scalable way to explore the vast space of Toffoli‑efficient circuits—a bottleneck that has limited practical algorithm deployment on near‑term hardware. The approach could accelerate the discovery of low‑overhead primitives for chemistry, optimization and number‑theoretic applications, though its success still depends on high‑quality evaluation metrics and may require further tuning to handle larger, more complex problems.

Significant efforts are currently being directed toward the implementation of large-scale quantum information processors, but realizing useful quantum advantage also requires the development of efficient quantum algorithms. While for many practical problems the dominant resource costs are associated with a small set of computational primitives, optimizing them in the quantum setting presents unique challenges, including a reversibility constraint absent from ordinary classical computation. Here we introduce an evolutionary framework in which large language models (LLMs) propose circuit designs and an independent evaluator verifies and scores them. We apply this framework to tasks spanning numerical computation, chemistry, optimization, quantum simulation, and number theory. In seven of the eight tasks, the discovered circuits significantly reduce both Toffoli and qubit counts relative to the state of the art. In the eighth, the search discovers a new reversible architecture for prime-field modular inversion. By handling reversibility differently, the architecture makes divsteps -- a classical algorithm previously impractical for reversible integer arithmetic -- viable and substantially improves the Toffoli-qubit trade-off for modular inversion. These results open the door for evaluator-guided LLM co-design of new algorithmic structures for quantum computation.

item.title: SynDebug: A Framework to Debug Logic Bugs in Fault-Tolerant Quantum Computing Programs
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article marks the first demonstration of a systems‑level debugging framework that works inside encoded fault‑tolerant quantum programs, filling a glaring gap left by earlier tools that only inspected logical circuits. By embedding lightweight assertion primitives directly into surface‑code–style QEC layers with an average depth penalty of just 1.8 % and no detectable rise in logical error rates, SynDebug makes it feasible to catch logic bugs before they explode into costly runtime failures—a crucial step as experimental groups move from small prototypes toward scalable FTQC architectures. The work dovetails with recent advances in real‑time syndrome processing and could accelerate the development cycle for large‑scale algorithms such as Shor’s or quantum chemistry, though its current validation is largely simulation‑based and will need hardware trials to confirm performance under realistic noise.

Fault-tolerant quantum computing (FTQC) introduces substantial systems-level complexity through quantum error correction (QEC), making debugging FTQC programs challenging. Existing quantum debugging approaches primarily target logical-level circuits and do not naturally support debugging within realistic FTQC execution flows. We present SynDebug, the first systems-level debugging framework for FTQC programs. SynDebug introduces lightweight assertion-based debugging primitives that operate directly within encoded FTQC infrastructures while avoiding additional logical surface area and minimizing temporal overhead. We evaluate SynDebug across multiple QEC code families, code distances, and encoded workloads, including state preparation, entanglement validation, and Shor-style programs. Our results demonstrate that SynDebug enables practical FTQC debugging with an average 1.8% additional circuit depth overhead (0% in most cases) and no measurable increase in the logical error rate, showing that systems-level debugging for large-scale FTQC applications is both feasible and practical.

item.title: Programmable all-to-all entangling gates for cavity-coupled atoms
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article demonstrates a cavity‑mediated Mølmer‑Sørensen gate that gives neutral‑atom qubits genuine all‑to‑all connectivity without shuttling atoms with optical tweezers, a long‑standing bottleneck for scaling up atom arrays. By leveraging the shared photonic mode and local laser addressing, the authors achieve >99 % fidelity while suppressing motional errors, bringing neutral‑atom platforms closer to the error‑rates needed for fault‑tolerant codes such as the surface code. The approach also dovetails with recent advances in Rydberg‑mediated gates and cavity QED, suggesting a clear path toward modular, high‑connectivity quantum processors that can be programmed on demand.

Fault tolerant quantum computers greatly benefit from having both high fidelity entangling gates and a non-local qubit connectivity. However, most entangling gates for neutral atoms are local, requiring separated atoms to be moved using optical tweezers to yield entanglement between them. Here, we design a high fidelity Mølmer Sørensen-like entangling gate between neutral atoms coupled to a photonic cavity, enabling a programmable all-to-all connectivity through the shared cavity coupling. The gate is both robust to changes in cavity photon number, and enables selective entanglement between any subset of separated atoms through local laser addressing. This eliminates the need to physically move atoms to perform the gate, and therefore motional errors and erasure are suppressed. Using experimentally realistic parameters we demonstrate gate fidelities exceeding $F > 0.99$, with higher fidelities achievable through optimal control of the pump amplitudes.

item.title: Efficient quantum simulation of unitary gates based on atomic ensembles
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article shows that permutation‑symmetric atomic ensembles can be turned into an efficient “qudit” platform by using a Cartan‑decomposition of the spin Hamiltonian, yielding compact circuits built from collective spin operations. By demonstrating zero‑error evolution that stays independent of atom number—unlike Suzuki‑Trotter methods whose errors grow with system size—the work offers a scalable route to high‑fidelity quantum simulation on near‑term hardware. The result could dramatically reduce gate depth for many‑body simulations, making larger ensemble‑based processors experimentally viable.

We develop a technique to perform efficient unitary time evolution of a general spin Hamiltonian based on the system with identical qubits, as naturally realized by permutation symmetric atomic ensembles. We employ Cartan decomposition method to the associated Hamiltonian Lie algebra and construct the symmetry adapted generators to implement unitary operator of the ensemble Hamiltonian. This enables the compact circuit representations of the system dynamics in terms of experimentally accessible collective spin operations and exploits the Dicke basis structure of the ensembles as an effective qudit representation. We benchmark Cartan based evolution against both exact time evolution and the Suzuki Trotter product formula. Our results show that the Cartan protocol accurately reproduces the operator dynamics, spin expectation values, and fluctuation observables with zero error that are substantially smaller than those obtained through Trotterization while maintaining an optimized circuit structure. In addition, scaling analysis with the ensemble size demonstrates that the Cartan error remains independent of the atom number while the corresponding Trotter error increases with the system size, highlighting the improved efficiency of the Cartan approach for a larger system size.

item.title: Classification of bipartite observables III: simplicity, mixtures and quantum error correction
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article shows that the infinite‑qubit Pauli group—central to stabilizer error correction—is mathematically the Fraïssé limit of finite alternating spaces, making it the exact analogue of the random graph in model theory. By interpreting simplicity theory as a language for quantum error correction, the authors reveal how Clifford circuits embody homogeneity, forking captures logical errors, and the Kim‑Pillay independence theorem mirrors syndrome gluing, offering a fresh logical toolkit for designing and analysing stabilizer codes. The work bridges abstract logic with practical QEC, suggesting new ways to reason about code structure and robustness while highlighting that once mixed preparations are allowed both frameworks acquire the tree property of the second kind, a subtle distinction that could inform future fault‑tolerant architectures.

The paradigm of a simple unstable theory in the sense of Shelah is the theory of the random graph, the Fraïssé limit of the finite graphs. Quantum error correction has a paradigm of its own, and we show that it is the counterpart of the random graph: the Pauli group on countably many qubits, taken modulo phases and with commutation as its relation, is the Fraïssé limit of the finite alternating spaces over the two-element field, and its form computes the syndromes of stabilizer codes. Seen through this correspondence, simplicity theory turns out to be a theory of error correction. Clifford encoding circuits implement the homogeneity of the Pauli group, forking recognizes the logical errors, and the independence theorem of Kim and Pillay is the gluing of syndromes. The two paradigms look alike as first-order structures, and they part company only when observables enter. Each defines a bipartite observable, and we prove that, once preparations are mixed, both acquire the tree property of the second kind in real-valued logic. They reach it by different roads, however, and we show that the probes decide which. The probes of the Pauli observable are the Pauli channels; for them the indicator of each syndrome sector is the difference of the responses of two uniform mixtures, and actual mixtures already witness the tree. The probes of the Rado observable see only marginals; conditions given by actual mixtures remain compatible on disjoint blocks, and the tree must be sought among idealized preparations.

item.title: Energetics of Fault-Tolerant Spin-Qubit Quantum Computation
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article is the first systematic accounting of how much power a fault‑tolerant silicon spin‑qubit processor would actually consume, showing that cryogenic cooling dominates the baseline budget and that control‑signal multiplexing can cut total energy by two orders of magnitude. By comparing the quantum Fourier transform to its classical FFT counterpart, the authors demonstrate that a quantum device could become energetically competitive well before it overtakes classical hardware in runtime—a key insight for scaling strategies that have so far focused almost exclusively on speed. The work ties together recent advances in isotopically purified silicon qubits and surface‑code error correction, providing designers with concrete targets for control electronics and cooling infrastructure as the field moves toward million‑qubit systems.

Semiconductor spin qubits offer a promising route to compact and scalable quantum computers, combining long coherence times in isotopically purified silicon with compatibility with semiconductor manufacturing. Beyond computational speedup, their energy efficiency is an important consideration for future large-scale systems. We evaluate the power and energy requirements of a Loss-DiVincenzo spin-qubit quantum computer by analyzing the Quantum Fourier Transform (QFT) and benchmarking it against the classical Fast Fourier Transform (FFT). We develop a detailed energy budget, identifying cryogenic cooling as the dominant baseline contribution before quantum error correction (QEC). The comparison between the QFT and the classical FFT reveals that, for any quantum workload operating under a polynomially bounded sampling regime, the crossover in energy consumption occurs at smaller problem sizes than the crossover in execution time. Thus, quantum computing can become energetically competitive before achieving a speedup in execution time. We then incorporate surface-code QEC and analyze the energy costs of QEC cycles, gate synthesis, and decoding. At scale, instrumentation and decoding become dominant contributions, while cryogenic cooling imposes a constraint on scalability. We show that optimizing the control-signal demultiplexing ratio can reduce the overall energy cost by approximately two orders of magnitude. For a system with about one million physical qubits, we estimate a power consumption of approximately 100 kW, at least one order of magnitude below that of today's highest-performance classical computing systems.

item.title: Connectivity Bounds for GHZ Graphs
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article settles a key open question about how the topology of photonic‑based GHZ experiments limits the dimensionality of multipartite entanglement, showing that vertex connectivity alone caps the achievable GHZ dimension by 2^{κ−1}+C(κ,2). By linking graph‑theoretic connectivity to concrete hardware constraints, the result narrows the search space for high‑dimensional GHZ sources and explains why many recent attempts have stalled at low dimensions. The bounds also give experimental designers a practical metric—improving network robustness directly translates into higher‑dimensional entanglement potential, though the limits still leave room for clever graph constructions to push beyond current records.

Greenberger-Horne-Zeilinger (GHZ) states are multipartite entangled quantum states that play a central role in quantum information theory, with applications in quantum communication, cryptography, and distributed quantum computing. A major experimental goal is to create high-dimensional GHZ states using multiple entangled parties. Krenn, Gu and Zeilinger discovered a surprising bridge between these quantum-optical experiments and graph theory: certain photonic experiments can be represented by edge-coloured, edge-weighted graphs, and the dimension of the produced GHZ state equals the number of feasible monochromatic inherited vertex colourings. This led Krenn and Gu to conjecture that every GHZ graph with more than four vertices has dimension at most $2$. A counterexample would give a new high-dimensional multipartite GHZ construction, while a proof would clarify fundamental resource limitations in quantum optics. It is known that the conjecture holds for graphs of vertex connectivity at most $2$ [MFCS 2024], and that simple GHZ graphs with $n>4$ vertices have dimension less than $n/\sqrt{2}$ [Quantum 2024]. However, no general upper bound depending only on vertex connectivity was known. We prove that every simple connected GHZ graph $G$ with at least four vertices has dimension at most $2^{κ(G)-1}+\binom{κ(G)}{2}$, where $κ(G)$ is the vertex connectivity of $G$. We also prove new bounds in terms of edge connectivity and maximum degree.

A white paper by Terra Quantum AG analyzes the vulnerability of major blockchain platforms like Bitcoin, Ethereum, and Solana to post-quantum cryptography (PQC) threats, highlighting the risks posed by Shor's algorithm to digital signature algorithms. The study evaluates PQC migration strategies, emphasizing signature payload size as a critical factor for high-throughput ledgers, and suggests FN-DSA (Falcon-512) as a viable solution due to its compact signature footprint. The paper also reviews mitigation frameworks, including Solana's WOTS vaults, Algorand's Falcon account roadmaps, and Ethereum's EIP-8052 proposal. Curator's Take: This article shows that hybrid quantum‑classical machine‑learning models can now deliver materially better predictions of atomic energies and forces while using far fewer resources than pure classical approaches, a milestone for quantum‑accelerated materials design. By embedding Quantum Depth‑Infused variational layers into the Allegro potential, Terra Quantum and Schaeffler demonstrate that even near‑term noisy devices can improve battery‑anode simulations such as copper‑lithium alloys, linking directly to industry‑relevant R&D. The work also highlights a practical advantage: hyperparameters trained on one dataset transfer cleanly to new materials, suggesting a path toward reusable quantum‑enhanced force fields. While the results are promising, scaling to larger, more complex systems will still require advances in qubit fidelity and error mitigation before widespread adoption.

Terra Quantum and Schaeffler have published a peer-reviewed study in Computational Materials Science on hybrid quantum machine learning for materials modeling. Their research demonstrates that a hybrid quantum-classical Allegro model, incorporating Quantum Depth-Infused (QDI) variational quantum circuit layers, significantly improves the accuracy of atomic energy and force predictions, particularly for copper-lithium structures relevant to battery anode research. This hybrid approach offers a substantial reduction in computational overhead while maintaining high accuracy, even when transferring hyperparameters to new datasets. item.title: Patchwork: automated lattice surgery and space-time partitioning for real-time decoding
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article matters because it delivers the first fully automated compiler—Patchwork—that can translate arbitrary multi‑qubit Pauli measurements into concrete lattice‑surgery operations on a realistic narrow‑corridor surface‑code layout, while preserving the full code distance even for logical Y measurements using twist defects. By introducing a wavefront partitioning scheme that separates commit, buffer and cleanup regions, the authors enable parallel, real‑time decoding whose failure rates closely match those of traditional monolithic decoders, addressing a major bottleneck in scaling fault‑tolerant processors. Together these tools bring practical, low‑latency error correction one step closer to large‑scale quantum computers that can run complex algorithms without prohibitive overhead.

We introduce patchwork, a lattice-surgery compiler for arbitrary multi-qubit Pauli measurements on a prescribed narrow-corridor two-dimensional surface-code layout. Systematic geometric rules simplify stabilizer placement and gate scheduling, including for logical $Y$ measurements implemented using twist defects. We introduce measurement circuits and schedules that, together with protruding lobes of $Y$-extension patches, preserve the full effective code distance for all numerically tested code distances. To support parallel decoding, we develop a wavefront algorithm that partitions merged lattice-surgery patches into space-time commit, buffer, and cleanup regions. Simulations of three sequential multi-qubit Pauli measurements acting on ten logical qubits show that staged decoding achieves total failure probabilities close to those of monolithic decoding over the parameters tested. These methods provide an automated framework for fault-tolerant lattice surgery and a route toward scalable, real-time decoding.

item.title: Operational Limits of Gravity-Mediated Entanglement
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article pinpoints the practical limits that finite‑size wave packets and stray forces impose on proposed gravity‑mediated entanglement experiments, moving the discussion from idealized point‑mass models toward realistic laboratory conditions. By quantifying when the generated state remains Bell‑nonlocal or useful for teleportation, it provides concrete design tolerances that complement recent tabletop proposals such as the Bose–Marletto–Vedral scheme and upcoming optomechanical tests. The finding that even a modest electrostatic coupling can cancel the gravitational phase underscores why meticulous shielding will be essential before any claim of witnessing quantum gravity can be made.

Tests of gravity-mediated entanglement aim to determine whether two massive objects in spatial superposition can become entangled through their mutual gravitational interaction. In an ideal model, the two objects are often treated as pointlike branches, but real wave packets have a finite width and are also exposed to dephasing and residual non-gravitational forces. We study these effects in a two-branch gravitational cat-state model with Gaussian wave packets. The Newtonian interaction is averaged over the finite wave-packet width, and spatially correlated dephasing is included phenomenologically. We then ask a practical question: when does the generated state remain useful rather than merely entangled? To answer this, we examine Bell violation, teleportation fidelity, coherent information, Fisher information, and state distinguishability. We find finite parameter windows where the same state is Bell-nonlocal and teleportation-useful, but these windows shrink as the wave packets become broader or the dephasing becomes stronger. We also show that a residual electrostatic branch interaction can coherently cancel the gravitational nonlocal phase and strongly suppress the operational signal. The results identify finite-width and electrostatic tolerance boundaries that should be considered in future tests of gravity-mediated entanglement.
